title: Best Credit Data Providers for Lenders: How to Compare and Combine Them
summary: The best credit data providers form a stack: consumer bureaus, business bureaus, and cash-flow data, combined so lenders decide faster.
body_markdown:
The best credit data providers for lenders include the three consumer credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion) and business bureaus such as Dun & Bradstreet. Most lenders also add alternative and verification data vendors, and the best mix depends on whether you lend to consumers, businesses, or both.


A credit data provider is a company that collects information about borrowers and sells it to lenders. Lenders use that information for underwriting, which is the process of deciding whether to approve a loan and on what terms.


A credit bureau is one type of provider that gathers payment history from lenders and other sources into credit reports. Bureaus supply the facts, but they do not approve or decline anyone, because that decision belongs to the lender's own credit policy and rules.


Bureau data alone also leaves gaps for some borrowers. The[CFPB credit invisibles update](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/data-research/research-reports/technical-correction-and-update-to-the-cfpbs-credit-invisibles-estimate/) says, "We estimate the share of the U.S. adult population who are credit invisible in 2020 to be 2.7 percent." Being credit invisible means a person has no credit record at all, and the same update found that many people once counted that way actually have a record that is too thin to score.


That is why the smartest way to think about "best" is as a stack of providers that work together. This guide explains the main provider types and how consumer and business data differ. It also shows how to evaluate the best credit data providers and combine them into one workflow.


### The Main Types of Credit Data Providers


Credit data providers fall into four broad groups: consumer bureaus, business bureaus, alternative and cash-flow data providers, and identity and fraud data providers. Each group answers a different question about the borrower, so most lenders use more than one.


The table below gives a quick summary of each group before we look at them one by one.


Provider Type Example Providers Best For Main Limitation


Consumer credit bureaus Equifax, Experian, TransUnion Personal loans, cards, and owner or guarantor checks Thin or missing files for some people


Business credit bureaus Dun & Bradstreet, Experian Business, Equifax Commercial, Creditsafe Trade payment history and company risk Young or small firms may have little data


Alternative and cash-flow data Bank transaction data (Plaid-type), rent and utility data, specialty bureaus Thin-file consumers and small businesses Needs borrower consent and careful analysis


Identity, KYB, and fraud data LexisNexis Risk Solutions, KYB vendors, The Work Number Verifying who the borrower is and what they earn Confirms identity but does not measure credit risk


#### Consumer Credit Bureaus: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion


The three credit bureaus are Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, and each one collects consumer credit data in the U.S. Each bureau builds credit reports from accounts that lenders and other companies choose to report to it.


Information on reports from the three bureaus may differ, so scores can differ too. Equifax offers a short explainer on[why bureau reports differ](https://www.equifax.com/personal/help/article-list/-/h/a/information-credit-report-credit-bureaus/) for readers who want more detail.


Here is what lenders typically rely on consumer bureaus for:


- **Payment history:** Shows whether a person has paid loans and cards on time and whether any accounts went to collections.
- **Credit use:** Shows how much of their available credit a person is using, which signals financial stress.
- **Public records and inquiries:** Shows recent applications for credit and certain public records tied to the person.


In small business lending, consumer bureaus still matter because many lenders check the owner or a guarantor. A guarantor is a person who promises to repay the loan if the business cannot. Instead of building three separate connections, lenders can reach all three bureaus through a[single credit bureau API](https://www.lendflow.com/post/credit-bureau-api) .


#### Business Credit Bureaus: Dun & Bradstreet, Experian Business, Equifax Commercial, Creditsafe


Business credit bureaus track companies instead of people. They collect trade payment data, which shows how a business pays its suppliers. They also track company details like size, industry, and years in business.


Businesses are tracked by business identifiers instead of a Social Security number (SSN). Dun & Bradstreet uses the D-U-N-S Number, a unique nine-digit ID assigned to each business location in its records.


D&B says its[Dun & Bradstreet Data Cloud](https://www.dnb.com/en-us/smb/duns/duns-and-companies.html) is a "Data Cloud of more than 600 million global businesses." That figure is D&B's own global record count, so it does not mean every listed business has a full credit file.


The[Dun & Bradstreet PAYDEX score](https://www.dnb.com/en-us/smb/resources/credit-scores/changes-to-dun-bradstreet-business-credit-scores.html) is an indicator of how promptly a company pays its suppliers and vendors.


Experian Business, Equifax Commercial, and Creditsafe are other examples of providers in the business credit bureau category. Their data can differ, so when ranking the best credit data providers for business lending, test each one against your own applicant list.


For a closer look at what these reports include, see our guide to[business credit report contents](https://www.lendflow.com/post/what-shows-up-on-a-business-credit-report) . Knowing those sections helps you decide which bureau fields your credit rules should actually use.


#### Alternative and Cash-Flow Data Providers


Alternative credit data is any information outside a traditional credit report that helps describe a borrower's finances. Common examples include bank account transactions, rent payments, utility bills, and data from specialty bureaus that focus on thin-file borrowers.


Cash-flow data is one type of alternative data used in small business lending. It comes from a borrower's bank account through bank data connection services, such as Plaid, and shows money coming in and going out over time.


This data is especially useful for thin-file small businesses, which are young or small companies with little or no business credit history. You can learn more about[combining cash-flow and bureau data](https://www.lendflow.com/post/plaid-underwriting) to build a fuller picture of these applicants.


Open banking is the practice of letting consumers share their bank data with third parties, such as lenders, through secure connections. The CFPB finalized its Section 1033 open banking rule in October 2024. The[CFPB open banking rule announcement](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/newsroom/cfpb-finalizes-personal-financial-data-rights-rule-to-boost-competition-protect-privacy-and-give-families-more-choice-in-financial-services/) listed "transaction information, account balance information, information needed to initiate payments, upcoming bill information, and basic account verification information."


As of April 2026, that rule is on hold and is not being enforced. Law firm Cozen O'Connor's update on the[open banking rule enjoined](https://www.cozen.com/news-resources/publications/2026/section-1033-compliance-date-open-banking-rule-enjoined-and-under-reconsideration) in federal court describes the status this way:


"A federal court has enjoined the CFPB from enforcing the rule while the Bureau undertakes a reconsideration process."


Because the final rule could change, lenders should check the Federal Register for updates before building plans around it. While the rule is reconsidered, lenders should confirm with their data partners and counsel how they access bank data.


#### Identity, KYB, and Fraud Data Providers


Identity and fraud data providers confirm that a borrower is real and is who they claim to be. KYC (know your customer) checks verify a person. KYB (know your business) checks verify that a business exists and that the applicant can act for it.


LexisNexis Risk Solutions is one example of a provider in the identity and fraud data category.[The Work Number from Equifax](https://www.equifax.com/newsroom/all-news/-/story/the-work-number-helps-unlock-opportunities-with-automated-employment-verification/) is an example of a provider in the income and employment verification category.


No single verification source finds every business, so many lenders use a verification waterfall. A waterfall checks one source first and moves to the next source only if the first one cannot confirm the match. Lendflow's[KYB waterfall Trust Score](https://www.lendflow.com/solutions/trust-score) uses this approach to check businesses across multiple verification sources.


### Consumer vs. Business Credit Data: Key Differences


Consumer and business credit data answer different questions, and they follow different rules. Consumer data tells you how a person manages debt, while business data tells you how a company pays its bills and how stable it is.


The table below compares the two side by side.


Feature Consumer Credit Data Business Credit Data


Main identifier Social Security number (SSN) D-U-N-S Number, EIN, or bureau file number


Main providers Equifax, Experian, TransUnion Dun & Bradstreet, Experian Business, Equifax Commercial, Creditsafe


Common scores Consumer credit scores such as FICO and VantageScore Business scores such as the Dun & Bradstreet PAYDEX score, an indicator of how promptly a company pays its suppliers and vendors


Key data Loans, cards, inquiries, collections Trade payments, company details, liens, and judgments


Federal law Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) Rules for business reports vary; ask your counsel


The FCRA is the federal law that controls how consumer credit reports are shared and used. The[Fair Credit Reporting Act text](https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/545A-FCRA-08-2022-508.pdf) says "any consumer reporting agency may furnish a consumer report under the following circumstances and no other." The same law also requires lenders that take adverse action based on a consumer report to give notice and name the reporting agency.


In plain terms, a bureau can share a consumer report only for reasons the law lists, which are called permissible purposes. Adverse action is a negative decision, such as a decline, and this overview is a general summary rather than legal advice.


Most small business lenders need both kinds of data, because the owner's personal credit and the company's payment history each reveal different risks. How the FCRA applies to owner and guarantor pulls is a detailed legal question, so review your process with counsel.


### How to Choose the Best Credit Data Providers: A Six-Step Framework


Choosing the best credit data providers starts with your borrowers, not with vendor marketing. A provider with huge coverage is only useful if it covers the people or companies who actually apply to you.


The market is large and varied, especially for small business lenders. According to[SBA small business statistics](https://advocacy.sba.gov/2026/02/03/advocacy-releases-frequently-asked-questions-about-small-businesses-2026/) , "There are 36,207,130 small businesses in the United States." The SBA defines a small business as one with fewer than 500 employees.


Use these six steps to evaluate each vendor:


1. **Coverage of your borrowers:** Check how many of your real applicants the provider can match, including young and very small businesses.
2. **Data methodology:** Ask where the data comes from, how records are matched, and how scores are built.
3. **Update frequency:** Confirm how often records refresh, since stale data can hide recent missed payments.
4. **Compliance support:** Confirm the provider supports FCRA duties, such as permissible purpose checks and the details needed for adverse action notices.
5. **API integration:** Review the API documentation, response speed, and data format your engineers will work with.
6. **Use-case fit:** Match each provider to a job, such as owner checks, business risk, cash flow, or fraud screening.


Before you sign a contract, ask each vendor for a sandbox, which is a test environment that returns sample or historical data. Run a batch of past applications through it and compare match rates and data quality. Then check how well the results line up with outcomes you already know.

Lendflow is not a credit bureau and does not replace your data providers. Instead, it is the orchestration and decisioning layer that connects your providers. Lendflow Connect handles data, Lendflow Intelligence handles decisions, and Lendflow Automate handles execution.


Even the best credit data providers cannot cover every borrower, every data type, and every risk on their own. Gaps are common in small business credit, where many applicants do not get all the funding they want. The[Fed Small Business Credit Survey](https://www.fedsmallbusiness.org/reports/survey/2026/2026-report-on-employer-firms) of employer firms reported these 2025 results from a convenience sample:


"Forty-two percent of applicants received the full amount of financing they sought, 36% received some or most, and 22% received none."


Data orchestration is the process of connecting many data sources and running them in the right order inside one workflow. A credit waterfall is a common orchestration pattern. The system calls a second provider only when the first one returns no match or too little data.


Orchestration also covers enrichment, which means adding outside data to an application so underwriters do not have to look it up by hand. With[automated borrower data enrichment](https://www.lendflow.com/solutions/data-enrichment) , bureau, business, and bank data can attach to each application as it arrives.


The final step is turning that data into a decision. An[automated credit decisioning engine](https://www.lendflow.com/solutions/credit-underwriting-and-decisioning) applies your credit rules to the combined data and returns an approval, a decline, or a referral for manual review.


Lendflow also lets lenders connect with top data partners in minutes and build decline waterfalls. A decline waterfall sends a declined application to the next lender or product that may fit, so fewer good deals are lost.


Here is what a combined provider stack might look like for three common lender types:


- **Consumer lender:** Pull one or more consumer bureaus, add identity checks, and use bank data for thin-file applicants.
- **Small business lender:** Combine a business bureau, an owner credit check, KYB verification, and cash-flow data from bank accounts.
- **Embedded finance platform:** Use one orchestration layer to route applicants across many lenders, each with its own data needs.


Lendflow's SMB Intelligence adds another layer beyond any single provider. It brings ecosystem-level signals, such as financing stacking, approval trends, and fraud indicators, that a lender cannot see from its own portfolio alone.


### Best Practices and Common Pitfalls


Even the best credit data providers can produce weak results if they are set up poorly. The practices below help you avoid frequent setup mistakes.


- **Pilot before contracting:** Test each provider with your own past applications before you commit to volume or long terms.
- **Map your entities:** Decide how you will link owners, guarantors, and businesses so data from each source matches the right applicant.
- **Avoid single-source dependence:** Keep a backup provider for each key data type, so an outage or coverage gap does not stall decisions.
- **Document adverse action and compliance:** Record which data drove each decline, so you can send accurate notices and pass audits.
- **Recheck regulatory status:** Review open banking and FCRA updates on a set schedule, since rules like Section 1033 may change.


The biggest pitfall is treating provider selection as a one-time purchase. Borrower mix, vendor coverage, and regulations all shift over time, so review your stack at least once a year.


### Conclusion


The best credit data providers are the ones that cover your actual borrowers and connect cleanly to your decisions. For most lenders, the best credit data providers form a mix of consumer bureaus, business bureaus, cash-flow data, and verification sources.


The real advantage comes from how you combine them. An orchestration and decisioning layer can run waterfalls, enrich applications, and turn complete data into faster, more consistent lending decisions.


### FAQs


These answers cover questions lenders often ask when comparing credit data providers. Each answer gives a short, direct starting point.


#### What Are the Three Main Credit Bureaus?


The three main credit bureaus in the U.S. are Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. Each one collects consumer credit data and sells credit reports to lenders.


#### Why Do Credit Scores Differ Between Bureaus?


Information on reports from the three bureaus may differ, so scores for the same person can differ too.


#### What Is a Business Credit Bureau API vs. a Consumer Credit API?


A business credit bureau API pulls company credit data, such as the PAYDEX score, an indicator of how promptly a company pays its suppliers and vendors. A consumer credit API pulls a person's credit report using details like an SSN and must follow FCRA permissible purpose rules.


#### How Do Lenders Assess Businesses With No Credit History?


Lenders often use cash-flow data from business bank accounts, KYB verification, and the owner's personal credit to assess businesses with thin or missing files. They combine these sources in one workflow to get a fuller view of risk.


#### What Criteria Should Guide Credit Data Provider Evaluation?


Focus on coverage of your borrowers, data methodology, update frequency, compliance support, API integration, and fit for each use case. Always test providers in a sandbox with your own applications before signing a contract.
